claims.text: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state has an intact native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel is a stable protective barrier at room temperature.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C causes the native oxide on Q235 steel to lose integrity.
High-temperature salt exposure transforms the oxide into a porous or spalled layer.
Breakdown of the native oxide exposes the underlying Q235 steel and accelerates its degradation.
Identical Q235 samples will be exposed to controlled aggressive salt atmospheres at room temperature and at 700–900 °C.
Inert-atmosphere controls at both temperature regimes can distinguish salt-induced degradation from thermal oxidation.
The protective native scale may consist of magnetite or a mixed oxide.
The microstructural integrity of the native oxide scale determines the degree of corrosion protection.
At room temperature, a dense and adherent native oxide limits ion transport and corrosion.
At high temperature, thermal stress and aggressive ionic interactions compromise the native oxide.
Oxide porosity or spallation permits corrosive species to reach the underlying steel and accelerates oxidation and degradation.
Room-temperature salt-exposed Q235 samples will show minimal mass change and limited corrosion.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 samples will show increased mass due to corrosion products.
High-temperature salt-exposed samples will exhibit greater oxide deterioration and substrate corrosion than room-temperature salt-exposed samples and inert controls.
Further alloying, surface treatment, or inhibitors may alter oxide formation or stability and make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Mass measurements, SEM/EDS, and XRD can assess corrosion-related mass change, oxide integrity, composition, and phase changes.
Failure of high-temperature salt-exposed samples to show greater mass change, oxide degradation, and internal corrosion than both comparison groups would falsify the proposed mechanism.
